summary: This document summarizes the 2016 Internet of Things Software Update workshop held in Dublin. It records the discussion of requirements, challenges and possible solutions for delivering software and firmware updates to small connected devices.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8240 is the report of a 2016 meeting about updating the software inside small connected devices. The participants set out what an update mechanism has to do, such as proving where an update came from, and recorded which questions were still open. It is a report of a discussion, not a specification.

subtitle: What a 2016 IAB workshop concluded about getting software and firmware updates onto small connected devices.

tldr.problem: Small connected devices are expected to run for 10 or more years, but they often ship with no way to receive a security fix, and no agreed mechanism exists for delivering and authorizing one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reports an IAB workshop that collected requirements for IoT software updates: data origin authentication, signed firmware images, partial updates, key rollover over a device lifetime, and ways to keep device identification private.
tldr.outcome: The workshop agreed that a standardized, signed update process would be an improvement, but designed no protocol. It listed next steps instead, including a way to transfer update authority when a maker stops supporting a device.

today: RFC 8240 is an Informational document published in September 2017. It records the discussions and recommendations of the 2016 IoTSU workshop, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it, so it stays as the account of what that meeting concluded rather than as a specification to implement.

sections.title: Why the Workshop Was Held
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) held a workshop on the Internet of Things Software Update (IoTSU) at Trinity College Dublin, Ireland on the 13th and 14th of June 2016. Its goal was to discuss requirements, challenges and solutions for delivering software and firmware updates to Internet-connected devices. This RFC is the report of that meeting.

The workshop brought together device vendors, security researchers, standards bodies and operators. It deliberately focused on constrained devices that run dedicated real-time operating systems, or no operating system at all, rather than on general-purpose systems such as a desktop running Linux.

The report states that the views it records are those of the workshop participants. They do not necessarily reflect the views of the participants' employers, of the authors, or of the IAB under whose auspices the workshop was held.

The call for position papers asked for material on protocol mechanisms for distributing updates, on securing those updates, on metadata about firmware packages, on the effect of operating system and hardware design, on installing updates, on privacy, and on the implications of device ownership and control.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is the written record of a two-day meeting in Dublin in June 2016 about updating the software inside small connected devices. It says what the participants wanted from an update process and, just as importantly, what they could not agree on.

sections.title: Device Classes and Update Types
sections.content:
Participants separated devices into two classes by processor type. A-class devices, built on ARM Cortex A-class or Intel Atom processors, are the kind found in set-top boxes and home routers; a Raspberry Pi is an A-class device able to run a regular desktop operating system such as Linux. M-class devices, built on ARM Cortex M-class or Intel Quark processors, are microcontrollers whose memory, flash and power budgets are tight. A-class processors are powerful enough for set-top boxes and home routers, and lower-end microcontrollers restrict how much software can be put on them at all.

The distinction decides what an update can look like. A-class devices can use the package managers known from the desktop and mobile world, such as Red Hat Package Manager (RPM) or pacman, which install and run each application in a compartmentalized way. A firmware update instead distributes the entire binary image, which consists of the operating system and all applications together. Most M-class devices use firmware updates, while A-class devices use a combination of firmware and software updates, with firmware updates being the less frequent operation.

The workshop also defined a hitless update: one applied in a way that does not impact the user experience. Applying an update can affect the user even when the device does not reboot, so an update applied when nobody is using the product is hitless.
sections.plainLanguage: The report splits devices into two kinds. A-class devices are powerful enough to run Linux, so they can install software package by package. M-class devices are small microcontrollers that usually take one complete firmware image instead. The smaller kind has far less room to work with.

sections.title: Requirements and Questions Raised
sections.content:
Participants agreed that data origin authentication (DAO) is required for software updates. Without it, updates simply become a perfect vulnerability. They also saw signing the firmware image itself, and the need for partial or differential updates, as important. A partial update sends only what changed rather than the whole firmware image, which may mean techniques such as bsdiff or Courgette, or may mean downloading a single application or library, which in turn may require dynamic linking and position independent code.

Other questions covered dependencies among software updates, including the hardware platform and configuration, and devices with multiple microcontrollers, where one microcontroller might handle the update service and dispatch software images to the others. Devices with several owners raised the question of who is authorized to push an update.

Signing raised further questions. The workshop asked whether digital signatures and encryption should be recommended as best current practice, and noted that not all low-end IoT devices use asymmetric cryptography, so for some device categories only a symmetric key approach seems viable. Simple symmetric schemes only show that the sender is a member of a group and do not fully authenticate a specific sender, and with a software update it is not wanted that a possibly compromised device can authenticate new software for all other similar devices. The workshop also asked how the firmware update signing key can be changed during a device's long lifetime, and whether one image may carry several signatures, for example one from the original equipment manufacturer and one from a certification body.

Further points included the need for secure storage to protect the update service's public key, a proposal not to send any new identifiers over an unencrypted channel during an update, minimizing device downtime and the energy spent on updates, and giving devices a reliable sense of the current time so they can check certificate validity.
sections.plainLanguage: The group agreed on one firm rule: an update has to prove where it came from, or the update path itself becomes a hole. Much else stayed open. They could not settle how to change the signing key on a device that lives for years, whether one image may need several signatures, or what to do about devices that cannot afford public-key cryptography.

sections.title: Authorizing an Update
sections.content:
Who may accept or reject an update was left as a question. The owner of a device, the user of it, or both may have a role, and the user is not necessarily the owner. For products that fall under a regulatory structure, such as healthcare, the workshop noted that firmware other than the accredited version should not be installed.

Not all updates are the same. Security updates are often treated differently from feature updates, and the authorization for them may differ too. Some people choose to decline updates, often because their system is currently stable, and possibly out of concern about unwanted changes; the workshop cited the HP printer firmware update pushed in March 2016 that turned off features end users liked.

Communicating that an update is available can also be hard. Doing so may require tracking the device and its status with regard to the installed firmware, with all the privacy downsides if such tracking is done badly.
sections.plainLanguage: The report leaves open who decides whether an update is applied, because the owner and the person using the device may be different people. It notes that a medical device should only run firmware that was accredited, and that users sometimes refuse updates that remove features they rely on.

sections.title: End-of-Support, Incentives and Device Tracking
sections.content:
Devices are often deployed for 10 or more years, and device makers may not want or be able to support software and services for that long, whether because of a change of business strategy caused by a merger, or because the company has gone bankrupt. The workshop asked whether it is technically possible to transfer device service to another provider, and cited the case of the Little Printer, where the community took over support after the source code was released, while observing that releasing source code does not by itself make others work on the code, fix bugs or maintain a service. Escrowing code so that a community can take it over was offered as one possible option. The session also noted that private signing keys may have to be made available in such a transfer, which could introduce security problems for already-deployed software and would change assumptions about the trust model.

Incentives were discussed separately. Companies that ship updates benefit from improved security, because their devices are less likely to be abused as a vector to launch other attacks, whether on their own networks or as part of a botnet. Updates can also break things, through service interruptions or through deliberate changes such as a feature that is no longer available. For most classes of device there does not seem to be a regulatory requirement to report or fix vulnerabilities, similar to data-breach-notification laws. Subscription models for device management were suggested so that the company providing the service has an economic interest in keeping devices online.

Three further subjects were recorded. On measurements, tracking deployed devices is hard because some connect only irregularly, and privacy-preserving statistical techniques such as RAPPOR and Intel's Enhanced Privacy ID were mentioned as ways to measure without exposing a unique identifier to anyone who asks. On firmware distribution in mesh networks, update can impose unacceptable performance burdens when there are many devices and some of them are sleepy, and the workshop found no clearly applicable standards-based multicast approach at the time. On compromised devices, prior IETF work including Network Endpoint Assessment and the bot remediation scheme of RFC 6561 had not found widespread deployment, so the conclusion was that there is interest in identifying and stopping misbehaving devices but the actual solution mechanisms are unclear.
sections.plainLanguage: A device may be in the field for ten years or more, and the company that made it may fold. The report asks whether someone else could take over the updates, including the signing keys. It also notes that nobody is required to fix vulnerabilities, so making updates worthwhile is as much a business question as a technical one.

sections.title: Conclusions and Next Steps
sections.content:
The participants recorded strong agreement that having some standardized secure software update, authorized and authenticated, would be an improvement over having none. They stopped short of proposing an entire update system: it is not clear that a whole system can or should be standardized, but there may be aspects where standards would help, such as metadata formats and protocols for distributing firmware updates.

The next steps named were installing updates with no operational interruption, distributing software updates without disrupting network operations in low-power wireless networks, including the development of a multicast transfer mechanism with appropriate security, a standard way to transfer authority and responsibility for updates, which the session described as very close to calling for a standard way to root devices as a feature of all devices, and documentation of proofs of concept for constrained devices on different operating system architectures, possibly in the IETF Light-Weight Implementation Guidance (lwig) Working Group.

The Security Considerations section notes that the whole report is security related, and that standardizing and deploying an update mechanism for IoT devices could help fix security vulnerabilities faster and, in some cases, be the only way to get a vulnerability patched at all. The document requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The group agreed that a standard, signed update process would be better than nothing, but it did not design one. The next steps it listed include a way to hand updates to a new owner when a maker disappears, a way to update without disturbing the network, and written examples for small devices.
